osces.title: Asthma/COPD Management and Spirometry Interpretation
learning_objectives: Interpret obstructive spirometry patterns with specific values
Differentiate between asthma and COPD management approaches
Demonstrate inhaler device techniques with Australian PBS medications
Apply appropriate oxygen saturation targets for COPD patients
Utilise COPD-X Guidelines and National Asthma Council recommendations

scenario.presenting_complaint: Worsening breathlessness and cough over 6 months
scenario.clinical_context: Current smoker (40 pack-years) with previous diagnosis of COPD, presenting for review of symptoms and spirometry results. Patient reports increased dyspnoea on exertion, morning cough with white sputum, and reduced exercise tolerance. He currently uses salbutamol PRN but struggles with technique.
scenario.background: Known COPD diagnosed 2 years ago following spirometry. Continues smoking 15 cigarettes daily. Previous hospital admission 12 months ago with acute exacerbation. Lives independently, works as a truck driver. No known allergies.

examination.respiratory: Reduced chest expansion, hyperresonant percussion, diminished breath sounds bilaterally, expiratory wheeze
examination.cardiovascular: Regular rhythm, no murmurs, no peripheral oedema
examination.other: Clubbing absent, accessory muscle use at rest

spirometry.interpretation: Severe obstructive pattern consistent with COPD exacerbation

investigations.chest_xray: Hyperinflation, flattened diaphragms, no acute consolidation
investigations.arterial_blood_gas: pH 7.38, PaCO2 48 mmHg, PaO2 58 mmHg, HCO3 28 mmol/L (chronic retention pattern)

tasks.instruction: Interpret the spirometry results and explain the findings to the patient
key_points: Results consistent with COPD with some asthmatic features

tasks.instruction: Demonstrate correct inhaler technique for prescribed medications
key_points: Common errors in inhaler use and correction

tasks.instruction: Discuss oxygen therapy targets and monitoring
key_points: COPD oxygen target 88-92% SpO2 (avoid oxygen toxicity)
Risk of CO2 retention with excessive oxygen
When to use supplemental oxygen therapy

tasks.instruction: Provide management plan following COPD-X Guidelines

immediate: Smoking cessation counselling and NRT prescription

medications.device_technique: Shake inhaler, exhale fully, seal lips around spacer, actuate once, inhale slowly and deeply, hold breath 10 seconds
Insert capsule into chamber, press button fully to pierce, inhale deeply and rapidly twice, check capsule is empty

criteria: States specific FEV1 and FVC values with percentages (5 marks)
Links findings to clinical presentation (5 marks)
Demonstrates MDI + spacer technique correctly (10 marks)
Identifies common errors and corrections (5 marks)
States correct SpO2 target for COPD (88-92%) (10 marks)
Explains rationale for controlled oxygen therapy (5 marks)
Discusses risks of excessive oxygen (5 marks)
Addresses smoking cessation as priority (10 marks)
Prescribes appropriate medications with PBS codes (10 marks)
Discusses pulmonary rehabilitation and vaccinations (5 marks)
Develops realistic exacerbation action plan (5 marks)

key_teaching_points: COPD oxygen targets differ from asthma (88-92% vs 94-98%)
Device technique is crucial for medication efficacy
Smoking cessation remains the most effective intervention
COPD-X Guidelines emphasise comprehensive management approach
common_mistakes: Applying standard oxygen targets (94-98%) to COPD patients
Focusing only on medications without addressing smoking
Missing the importance of pulmonary rehabilitation

australian_guidelines: National Asthma Council Australia - COPD Management
learning_resources: COPD-X concise guide for primary care
National Asthma Council inhaler technique videos
Lung Foundation Australia patient education materials

osces.title: Asthma/COPD Management and Spirometry Interpretation
learning_objectives: Interpret spirometry findings in obstructive lung disease
Differentiate between asthma and COPD based on clinical features
Demonstrate appropriate inhaler technique with device selection
Apply appropriate oxygen therapy targets
Formulate evidence-based management plan using Australian guidelines
osces.scenario_description: Mrs Jennifer Chen, a 58-year-old Chinese-Australian woman, presents to your respiratory clinic with increasing breathlessness over the past 3 months. She has a 30 pack-year smoking history (quit 5 years ago) and works as a high school chemistry teacher. She reports morning cough with clear sputum, wheeze on exertion, and difficulty climbing stairs. Her GP has referred her following spirometry results. You need to interpret her lung function tests, assess her symptoms, and formulate an appropriate management plan.
osces.presenting_complaint: Progressive dyspnoea on exertion with morning cough over 3 months
osces.history_of_presenting_illness: Mrs Chen reports gradual onset of breathlessness when climbing stairs or walking uphill over the past 3 months. She experiences a productive cough most mornings with small amounts of clear sputum. Occasionally hears wheeze during physical activity. No chest pain or haemoptysis. Symptoms are worse on cold mornings and during school term when exposed to chemical fumes in the laboratory. She uses her reliever inhaler 3-4 times per week, increased from once weekly 6 months ago.
past_medical_history: Osteoporosis (post-menopausal, on calcium and vitamin D)
medications: Salbutamol 100mcg MDI PRN (current use 3-4 times weekly)

social_history.occupation: High school chemistry teacher (potential occupational exposures)
social_history.exercise: Previously walked 5km daily, now limited by breathlessness

osces.family_history: Father had emphysema (heavy smoker), mother with late-onset asthma

examination_findings.general: Comfortable at rest, no accessory muscle use

respiratory.inspection: Barrel chest shape, pursed lip breathing on exertion demonstration
respiratory.auscultation: Reduced air entry bilaterally, expiratory wheeze on forced expiration, no crackles

examination_findings.cardiovascular: Dual heart sounds, no murmurs, JVP not elevated
examination_findings.other: No finger clubbing, no peripheral oedema

post_bronchodilator.reversibility: FEV1 improvement 17% (300mL), consistent with significant reversibility

investigations.chest_xray: Hyperinflated lung fields, flattened diaphragms, no focal consolidation
investigations.full_blood_count: Hb 138 g/L, WCC 7.2 x10^9/L, Eosinophils 0.15 x10^9/L (normal)
investigations.specific_ige: House dust mite RAST class 3, cat dander RAST class 2

key_clinical_features: Significant smoking history with obstructive spirometry pattern
Elevated total IgE with specific environmental allergen sensitisation
Mixed features of asthma and COPD (Asthma-COPD Overlap - ACO)

immediate: Assess current inhaler technique with salbutamol MDI
Oxygen saturation monitoring - target 94-98% (asthma component predominant)
Peak flow monitoring diary for 2 weeks

pharmacological.device_technique: Demonstrate slow, deep inhalation with spacer device, hold for 10 seconds
Load dose, breathe out, forceful deep inhalation, hold breath 10 seconds
Pierce capsule, inhale deeply twice from same capsule, ensure capsule rattles

non_pharmacological: Allergen avoidance strategies (house dust mite, pets)
Occupational health assessment regarding chemical exposures
monitoring: Spirometry review in 3 months post-treatment initiation
Asthma Control Test (ACT) score at each visit
Bone density monitoring due to ICS therapy

red_flags.action: Consider alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, urgent respiratory referral
Urgent chest CT and respiratory referral to exclude malignancy

red_flags.flag: Severe exacerbation with type 2 respiratory failure
red_flags.action: Controlled oxygen therapy 88-92% if COPD features predominant, BiPAP consideration

guidelines_referenced: National Asthma Council Australia - Australian Asthma Handbook
TSANZ Position Statement on ACO (Asthma-COPD Overlap)
learning_points: ACO represents patients with features of both asthma and COPD requiring dual therapy approaches
Significant reversibility (>12% and >200mL FEV1 improvement) suggests asthmatic component
Occupational exposures can trigger both asthma and COPD exacerbations
Triple therapy (ICS/LABA/LAMA) is first-line for ACO patients
Oxygen targets depend on predominant phenotype - 94-98% for asthma, 88-92% for COPD

history_taking: Reviews previous asthma history and control
investigation_interpretation: Correctly interprets spirometry values and pattern
Integrates imaging findings with clinical picture
management_planning: Demonstrates appropriate inhaler technique for different devices

common_mistakes: Incorrectly targeting 88-92% oxygen saturation when asthmatic component predominates
Poor inhaler technique demonstration, especially with HandiHaler capsule system
Failure to recognise ACO as distinct from pure asthma or COPD
Not addressing occupational triggers in management plan
Inadequate smoking cessation counselling and support
extensions: Discuss indications for home oxygen therapy
Explain criteria for pulmonary rehabilitation referral
Review vaccination recommendations for COPD patients
Describe when to consider bronchoscopy or high-resolution CT

scenario.patient_background: Margaret Chen, a 58-year-old former coal miner presenting with progressive breathlessness and chronic cough. She has a 40 pack-year smoking history, quit 5 years ago. Recently hospitalized for respiratory exacerbation requiring antibiotics and prednisolone.
scenario.chief_complaint: Worsening shortness of breath over the past 6 months, particularly on exertion
scenario.context: Patient referred by GP for specialist assessment and optimization of respiratory management. Recent spirometry and chest X-ray available.

osces.task_description: Conduct a focused respiratory consultation including history taking, clinical examination, spirometry interpretation, and management planning for this patient with suspected COPD exacerbation.
learning_objectives: Demonstrate systematic approach to respiratory history taking including occupational exposure assessment
Perform focused respiratory examination with attention to signs of airflow obstruction
Interpret spirometry results and classify severity of obstruction
Formulate appropriate management plan including inhaler therapy optimization
Demonstrate proper inhaler technique and patient education
Apply Australian COPD-X guidelines for management recommendations
assessment_criteria: History taking: Comprehensive respiratory history including smoking history, occupational exposures, and symptom progression (25%)
Physical examination: Systematic respiratory examination with correct technique and identification of relevant signs (25%)
Clinical reasoning: Accurate interpretation of investigations and formulation of differential diagnosis (20%)
Management planning: Appropriate therapeutic recommendations based on COPD-X guidelines (20%)
Communication: Clear explanation of diagnosis and treatment plan to patient (10%)

patient_presentation.appearance: Well-groomed woman appearing her stated age, sitting upright, mild pursed-lip breathing at rest

history.presenting_complaint: Progressive dyspnea on exertion over 6 months, now SOB climbing one flight of stairs. Daily productive cough with white-yellow sputum, worse mornings. Two respiratory 'flare-ups' requiring antibiotics in past year.
history.past_medical_history: Hypertension, osteoporosis, previous pneumonia 2018. No previous formal COPD diagnosis.
history.medications: Amlodipine 5mg daily, alendronate 70mg weekly, ventolin MDI PRN (uses 2-3 times daily)
history.social_history: 40 pack-year smoking history (quit 2019), worked in coal mine for 25 years (1985-2010), lives with husband in single-story home, retired cleaner
history.family_history: Father died of 'lung problems', mother had asthma

examination_findings.general: Alert, cooperative, mild respiratory distress, no clubbing or cyanosis
examination_findings.respiratory: Barrel chest configuration, reduced chest expansion bilaterally, hyperresonant percussion throughout, diminished breath sounds bilaterally with expiratory wheeze, prolonged expiratory phase
examination_findings.cardiovascular: Regular rhythm, no murmurs, elevated JVP 6cm, mild peripheral edema

spirometry.interpretation: Severe obstructive pattern consistent with COPD. Post-bronchodilator FEV1 improvement 8% (below significant reversibility threshold).

investigations.chest_xray: Hyperinflation with flattened diaphragms, increased retrosternal air space, no consolidation or masses
investigations.arterial_blood_gas: pH 7.38, pCO2 48 mmHg, pO2 58 mmHg, HCO3 28 mmol/L on room air
investigations.full_blood_count: Hemoglobin 148 g/L, WCC 7.2 x10⁹/L, platelets 245 x10⁹/L

osces.diagnosis: COPD GOLD Stage 3 with features of chronic bronchitis, likely occupational component (pneumoconiosis). Current mild exacerbation.

immediate: Optimize bronchodilator therapy with dual long-acting bronchodilators
Target oxygen saturation 88-92% given COPD and CO2 retention risk
Smoking cessation counseling and support (Quitline referral)

medications.technique: Demonstrate HandiHaler use: pierce capsule, inhale deeply and slowly, hold breath 10 seconds
Shake inhaler, exhale fully, actuate into spacer, inhale slowly and deeply, hold breath 10 seconds

medications.indication: Combination LABA/ICS for severe COPD with exacerbation history
medications.technique: Load dose, exhale away from device, inhale forcefully and deeply through mouthpiece

medications.indication: Short course for current mild exacerbation
medications.monitoring: Monitor blood glucose if diabetic, review after course completion

non_pharmacological: Pulmonary rehabilitation referral - 6-8 week supervised program
Annual influenza vaccination and pneumococcal vaccination
Home oxygen assessment if symptoms persist despite optimal therapy
COPD action plan education for early exacerbation recognition
management_plan.follow_up: Review in 4-6 weeks post medication optimization, earlier if symptoms worsen

key_teaching_points: COPD diagnosis requires post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC <0.70 with appropriate clinical context
Occupational history crucial - coal mining is significant risk factor for pneumoconiosis and COPD
Oxygen target 88-92% in COPD patients due to CO2 retention risk
Dual bronchodilator therapy (LAMA + LABA) first-line for GOLD Stage 3
ICS/LABA combination indicated for frequent exacerbators (≥2 per year or ≥1 requiring hospitalization)
Proper inhaler technique essential - up to 90% of patients use inhalers incorrectly
Pulmonary rehabilitation improves exercise capacity and quality of life in COPD
common_mistakes: Failing to identify occupational exposure history
Incorrect oxygen saturation targets (using 94-98% instead of 88-92%)
Prescribing ICS monotherapy instead of combination bronchodilators
Missing signs of cor pulmonale (elevated JVP, peripheral edema)
Inadequate assessment of exacerbation triggers and action plan education

examination_focus: Inspection for barrel chest and breathing pattern
Palpation for chest expansion and tactile fremitus
Auscultation for wheeze and prolonged expiration
Assessment for signs of right heart strain
expected_management: Recognition of severe COPD based on spirometry

osces.scenario: Mrs. Patricia Chen, 58-year-old office worker, presents to your clinic with worsening breathlessness and morning cough. She has a 30 pack-year smoking history (quit 2 years ago) and reports increased wheeze over the past month. Current medications include salbutamol MDI 'as needed'. Recent spirometry shows FEV1 1.8L (45% predicted), FVC 3.2L (65% predicted), FEV1/FVC 0.56.

patient_presentation.chief_complaint: Worsening breathlessness and morning cough over past month
patient_presentation.history_of_presenting_illness: Mrs. Chen reports progressive dyspnoea on exertion, particularly climbing stairs to her second-floor office. Morning cough productive of clear sputum, worse on waking. Increased wheeze audible to herself. Uses salbutamol 3-4 times daily (previously once weekly). No fever, chest pain, or haemoptysis. Sleep disturbed by cough twice weekly.
patient_presentation.past_medical_history: Hypertension (well-controlled on perindopril), osteoarthritis knees. No previous hospital admissions for respiratory illness.
patient_presentation.medications: Salbutamol 100mcg MDI PRN, perindopril 5mg daily, paracetamol PRN
patient_presentation.social_history: 30 pack-year smoking history, ceased 2 years ago. Works in accounting, minimal occupational dust exposure. Lives with husband in two-storey home. Independent with ADLs.
patient_presentation.family_history: Mother had 'emphysema', father died of myocardial infarction age 72

physical_examination.general_appearance: Comfortable at rest, no acute distress. Able to speak in full sentences.

respiratory_examination.inspection: Mild use of accessory muscles on deep inspiration. No finger clubbing. Chest wall symmetrical.
respiratory_examination.palpation: Reduced chest expansion bilaterally. Vocal fremitus normal.
respiratory_examination.auscultation: Widespread wheeze on expiration, reduced air entry bibasally. Prolonged expiratory phase.

physical_examination.cardiovascular_examination: Heart sounds dual, no murmurs. No peripheral oedema. JVP not elevated.
physical_examination.other_systems: Abdomen soft, non-tender. No hepatosplenomegaly. Neurological examination deferred.

spirometry.interpretation: Moderate obstructive pattern consistent with COPD. Post-bronchodilator FEV1 improvement 180ml (reversibility 10%)

investigations.chest_xray: Hyperinflated lung fields. Flattened diaphragms. No consolidation or pleural effusion.
investigations.full_blood_count: Hb 128 g/L, WCC 6.8 x10^9/L, platelets 285 x10^9/L
investigations.arterial_blood_gas: pH 7.41, pCO2 42 mmHg, pO2 68 mmHg, HCO3 26 mmol/L (room air)

diagnosis.primary: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD), moderate severity with exacerbation

immediate: Oxygen therapy to maintain SpO2 88-92% (COPD-specific target to avoid CO2 retention)

medications.instructions: Demonstrate MDI + spacer technique: shake inhaler, breathe out, seal lips around spacer, press canister once, breathe in slowly and deeply, hold breath 10 seconds
Demonstrate HandiHaler technique: open capsule chamber, insert capsule, close, press green button to pierce, breathe out, seal lips around mouthpiece, breathe in rapidly and deeply
Take with food, complete full course even if feeling better

non_pharmacological: Action plan development for exacerbation management
follow_up: Review in 1 week to assess response to treatment
COPD Assessment Test (CAT) score baseline and monitoring

key_teaching_points: COPD oxygen targets are 88-92% SpO2 to prevent hypercapnic respiratory failure
Long-acting bronchodilators (LABA/LAMA) are first-line maintenance therapy per COPD-X Guidelines
Inhaler device technique is crucial - patients require demonstration and regular review
COPD exacerbations often triggered by viral infections - early recognition and treatment important
Pulmonary rehabilitation improves exercise capacity and quality of life in COPD
examiner_notes: Assess candidate's ability to interpret spirometry and recognise obstructive pattern
Observe inhaler technique demonstration - common examination focus
Test knowledge of COPD-specific oxygen saturation targets
Evaluate understanding of stepwise COPD management per Australian guidelines
Look for appreciation of smoking cessation as key intervention
australian_guidelines_referenced: COPD-X Guidelines (Lung Foundation Australia/Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand)
National Asthma Council Australia - COPD management
Royal Australian College of General Practitioners - COPD
learning_objectives: Interpret spirometry results and classify COPD severity
Demonstrate correct inhaler techniques for MDI + spacer and dry powder devices
Apply appropriate oxygen saturation targets for COPD patients
Develop comprehensive COPD management plan including exacerbation treatment
Counsel patients on smoking cessation and non-pharmacological interventions
red_flags: SpO2 < 88% on room air requiring immediate oxygen therapy
Signs of respiratory failure: confusion, exhaustion, paradoxical breathing
Pneumothorax: sudden chest pain with absent breath sounds
Pneumonia: fever, consolidation on examination, purulent sputum
